title: Continuous-Variable MIMO THz Quantum Secret Sharing: Gaussian-modulation and Passive-modulation
authors: Leixin Wu, Jiayu Pan, Fangzhe Chen, Lingtao Zhang, Bowen Zheng, Tie Qiu
abstract: Although quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure key distribution, it is mainly designed for point-to-point communication and cannot directly support multi-user collaborative scenarios. To address this limitation, quantum secret sharing (QSS) has been proposed to enable secure multiparty key sharing. However, most existing QSS protocols rely on a single-input single-output (SISO) channel, which limits the achievable secret key rate (SKR) and transmission distance. This paper proposes a continuous-variable (CV) QSS protocol based on a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architecture operating in the terahertz (THz) band. In the proposed scheme, transmit-receive beamforming decomposes the MIMO channel into multiple parallel SISO subchannels, thereby improving both the SKR and transmission distance. We describe the QSS transmission procedure and derive the SKR expressions for eight protocol variants under Gaussian collective attacks. Specifically, Gaussian modulation and passive modulation are considered at the transmitter, while homodyne and heterodyne detection are considered at the receiver. Both asymptotic and composable finite-size SKR formulas are derived to characterize the ideal upper-bound performance and the achievable performance under finite resources, respectively. Simulation results show that, under ideal assumptions including perfect channel state information, perfect phase synchronization, and ideal beamforming, the Gaussian-modulation protocol with a 32 x 32 antenna configuration and the passive-modulation protocol with a 1024 x 1024 antenna configuration achieve transmission distances of 14.99 m and 160 m in the atmospheric channel, respectively. These results provide an idealized theoretical benchmark for evaluating the potential performance gains of MIMO-assisted THz CV-QSS in indoor and short-range outdoor wireless networks.
summary: This paper proposes a novel Continuous-Variable Quantum Secret Sharing protocol leveraging a MIMO architecture operating in the THz band to overcome the limitations of point-to-point QKD. By decomposing the channel via beamforming and analyzing both Gaussian and passive modulation schemes, it derives theoretical benchmarks showing significant improvements in key rate and transmission distance for multi-user quantum communication.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) being point-to-point by proposing a multi-user Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) protocol.
main_result: The proposed MIMO architecture significantly improves both the achievable Secret Key Rate (SKR) and transmission distance compared to conventional SISO schemes in the THz band.
method: It utilizes transmit-receive beamforming to decompose the MIMO channel into parallel SISO subchannels, analyzing eight protocol variants under Gaussian collective attacks.
model_or_system: The system is a Continuous-Variable (CV) QSS protocol operating over an atmospheric channel using a Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) architecture in the Terahertz (THz) band. It compares Gaussian Modulation (GMCS) and Passive Modulation (PMCS).
key_observables: Secret Key Rate (SKR), transmission distance, and minimum net secure key bits shared per MIMO-QSS round.

main_assumptions: Simulation results assume ideal conditions like perfect Channel State Information (CSI), phase synchronization, and beamforming; the analysis also incorporates thermal noise for physical realism.

paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for multi-user QSS over MIMO channels. It details the transmission procedure involving beamforming, modulation (GMCS/PMCS), detection (homodyne/heterodyne), and subsequent classical post-processing steps to derive SKR expressions. Finally, it derives formulas for composable finite-size SKRs.
why_interesting: The work pushes quantum communication into high-frequency regimes (THz) using advanced MIMO techniques, which is crucial for realizing practical quantum networks in challenging wireless environments.
